# A quick overview before our last lecture!

## How to deal with uncertainty?

![](images/slot-machine.jpg){.absolute .fragment top="300" right="80" width="35%"}

::: incremental
-   So far, we have seen [different tools]{style="color: purple;"} to communicating an uncertain outcome (i.e., a [random variable]{style="color: purple;"}):

    -   Probability mass or density function.
    -   Odds.
    -   Mode.
    -   Entropy.
    -   Mean.
    -   Variance/standard deviation.
:::

### However...

-   Sometimes, it is [difficult]{style="color: purple;"} to compute them.
-   In these situations, we can use [simulation]{style="color: purple;"}.

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width="25%"}

![](images/code.png){.absolute .fragment top="200" right="280" width="10%"}

-   Note this lecture will be conducted in `R` and `Python`.

# Today's Learning Goals

## By the end of this lecture, we will be able to...

-   Generate a random sample from a discrete distribution in both `R` and `Python`.
-   Reproduce the same random sample each time you re-run your code in either `R` or `Python` by setting the seed or random state. 
-   Evaluate whether or not a set of observations are independent and identically distributed (*iid*).

## And...

-   Use simulation to approximate distribution properties (e.g., mean and variance) using empirical quantities, especially for random variables involving multiple other random variables.
-   Argue why simulations can approximate true properties of a stochastic quantity.

# Outline

1.  Review on Random Samples
2.  Seeds
3.  Generating Random Samples: Code
4.  Running Simulations
5.  Multi-Step Simulations

## 1. Review on Random Samples

-   A [random sample]{style="color: purple;"} is a collection of random outcomes/variables.
-   A random sample of size $n$ is usually depicted as $X_1, \ldots, X_n$.

. . .

-   Some examples of random samples are listed as follows:
    -   The outcomes of ten dice rolls ([$n = 10$]{style="color: purple;"}).
    -   The daily high temperature in Vancouver for each day of the year ([$n = 365$]{style="color: purple;"}).

### Heads-up!

![](images/crab.png){.absolute top="-120" right="100" width="20%"}

::: incremental
-   [Unless we make additional sampling assumptions]{style="color: purple;"}, a [default]{style="color: purple;"} random sample is said to be [independent and identically distributed]{style="color: purple;"} (or [iid]{style="color: purple;"}).
-   Moreover, the word [stochastic]{style="color: purple;"} refers to having some uncertain outcome.
-   The opposite of stochastic is [deterministic]{style="color: purple;"}: an outcome that will be known with 100% certainty.
:::

## 2. Seeds

![](images/farmers.png){.absolute top="20" right="-100" width="20%"}

. . .

-   Computers cannot actually generate truly random outcomes.
-   Instead, they use something called [[pseudorandom numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudorandom_number_generator)]{style="color: purple;"}.

. . .

-   As an example of a [basic algorithm]{style="color: purple;"} that produces pseudo-random numbers between 0 and 1, [consider starting with your choice of number $x_0$ between 0 and 1]{style="color: purple;"}, and iterating the following equation:

$$x_{i+1} = 4 x_i (1 - x_i).$$

### The output

![](images/code.png){.absolute top="-120" right="100" width="20%"}

-   Random numbers between 0 and 1.
-   For example, here is the resulting sequence when we start with $x_0 = 0.3$ and iterate $n = 1000$ times:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
n <- 1000
x <- 0.3
for (i in 1:n) x[i + 1] <- 4 * x[i] * (1 - x[i])
head(x)
```

### Plotting values from vector `x`

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

library(tidyverse)

n <- 1000
x <- 0.3
for (i in 1:n) x[i + 1] <- 4 * x[i] * (1 - x[i])

qplot(0:n, x) +
  labs(
    x = "Iteration Number",
    y = "Function Evaluation"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 20),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 20)
  )
```

### Some additional highlights!

![](images/code.png){.absolute top="-70" right="0" width="15%"}

. . .

-   Although the previous sequence is [deterministic]{style="color: purple;"}, it behaves like a random sample.
-   [But not entirely!]{style="color: purple;"} All pseudorandom number generators have some pitfalls.

. . .

-   In this example, one pitfall is that neighbouring pairs [are not independent of each other]{style="color: purple;"}.

### The seed or random state

![](images/seed.jpg){.absolute top="-70" right="0" width="15%"}

::: incremental
-   The [seed]{style="color: purple;"} (or [random state]{style="color: purple;"}) in a pseudo-random number generator is some pre-specified initial value that determines the generated sequence.
-   In `R`, we can set the seed using the [`set.seed()`](https://www.statology.org/set-seed-in-r/) function.
-   In `Python`, we can use [`numpy.random.seed()`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/generated/numpy.random.seed.html) from `numpy`.
-   The seed gives us an added advantage over truly random numbers: it allows our analysis to be [reproducible]{style="color: purple;"}!
:::

## 3. Generating Random Samples: Code

-   We will look at some `R` and `Python` functions that help us generate a random sample.
-   Note we are still focusing on discrete distributions here.

![](images/code.png){fig-align="center" width="15%"}

## 3.1. From Finite Number of Categories

-   In `R`, we can generate a random sample from a [discrete distribution]{style="color: purple;"} with a finite number of outcomes using the [[`sample()` function](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/base/versions/3.6.2/topics/sample)]{style="color: purple;"}.

. . .

-   In `Python`, we can generate a random sample from a discrete distribution using the [[`numpy.random.choice()` function](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/random/generated/numpy.random.choice.html)]{style="color: purple;"}.

> **Heads-up:** Note that both `R` and `Python` have their own algorithms to generate pseudorandom outcomes, **even though we provide the same seed**.

### How does `sample()` work in `R`?

. . .

-   Put the outcomes as a vector in the first argument, `x`.
-   Put the desired sample size in the argument `size`.
-   Put `replace = TRUE` [so that sampling can happen with replacement]{style="color: purple;"}.
-   Put the probabilities of the outcomes as a vector respective to `x` in the argument `prob`.

. . .

> **Heads-up**: If these probabilities do not add up to 1, `R` **will not** throw an error. Instead, `R` automatically adjusts the probabilities so that they add up to 1.

#### `R` Example

-   Here is an example of generating $n = 10$ items using the Mario Kart item distribution from `lecture1`.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
outcomes <- c("banana", "bob-omb", "coin", "horn", "shell")
probs <- c(0.12, 0.05, 0.75, 0.03, 0.05)
n <- 10
sample(outcomes, size = n, replace = TRUE, prob = probs)
```

### How does `numpy.random.choice()` work in `Python`?

. . .

-   Put the outcomes in the first argument, `a`.
-   Put the desired sample size in the argument `size`.
-   Put the probabilities of the outcomes respective to `x` in the argument `p`.

. . .

> **Heads-up:** In `numpy.random.choice()`, it is necessary that the probabilities in `prob` add up to 1.

#### `Python` Example

-   Using the Mario Kart example again, we have the following:

```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
import numpy

numpy.random.seed(551)
outcomes = ["banana", "bob-omb", "coin", "horn", "shell"]
probs = [0.12, 0.05, 0.75, 0.03, 0.05]
n = 10
numpy.random.choice(a = outcomes, size = n, p = probs)
```

## 3.2. From Distribution Families

::: incremental
-   In `R`, we can generate data from a distribution belonging to [some parametric family]{style="color: purple;"} using the `rdist()` function, where "`dist`" is replaced with a short form of the distribution family's name.
-   In `Python`, we can use the `stats` module from the `scipy` library.
:::

### Function Summary

![](images/code-2.png){.absolute top="-70" right="0" width="12%"}

-   The table below summarizes the functions related to some of the discrete distribution families we have seen.

|      Family       | `R` Function |      `Python` Function      |
|:-----------------:|:------------:|:---------------------------:|
|     Binomial      |  `rbinom()`  |  `scipy.stats.binom.rvs()`  |
|     Geometric     |  `rgeom()`   |  `scipy.stats.geom.rvs()`   |
| Negative Binomial | `rnbinom()`  | `scipy.stats.nbinom.rvs()`  |
|      Poisson      |  `rpois()`   | `scipy.stats.poisson.rvs()` |

### How to use these functions?

::: incremental
-   Sample size:
    -   For `R`, put this in the argument `n`, which comes first.
    -   For `Python`, put this in the argument `size`, which comes last.
-   In both languages, each parameter has its own argument.
-   Sometimes, like in `R`'s `rnbinom()`, [we have the option for different parameterizations]{style="color: purple;"}.
-   Be sure only to specify the [exact number of parameters]{style="color: purple;"} required to isolate a member of the distribution family!
:::

### Binomial Example

-   $n = 10$ random numbers with $p = 0.6$ and 5 trials.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
rbinom_output <- rbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.6)
rbinom_output
```

```{pyodide-python}
#| autorun: true
import scipy
numpy.random.seed(551)
scipy.stats.binom.rvs(n = 5, p = 0.6, size = 10)
```

### Heads-up!

![](images/crab.png){.absolute top="-80" right="-80" width="20%"}

::: incremental
-   Let us not confuse the [random sample size]{style="color: purple;"} $n$ (i.e., `n` in any `R` function to generate random numbers) with the number of trials $n$ as a parameter of a Binomial random variable (i.e., `size` in `rbinom()`).
-   For `Python`, the Binomial parameter $n$ is actually depicted as `n` and `size` is the number of Binomial random numbers in our sample.
:::

### Negative Binomial Example

-   The Negative Binomial family is an example of a function in `R` that allows different parameterizations.

. . .

-   Suppose the following:

$$X \sim \text{Negative Binomial} (k, p).$$

-   $X$ refers to the number of failures in [independent successive Bernoulli trials before experiencing $k$ successes with probability $p$]{style="color: purple;"}.

#### `R` Function `rnbinom()`

<br>

-   This function generates `n` Negative Binomial-distributed random numbers with arguments `size` as $k = 5$ and `prob` as $p = 0.6$:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
rnbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.6)
```

</br>

#### Heads-up!

-   Notice that specifying [too few parameters]{style="color: purple;"} results in an [error]{style="color: purple;"} (recall, we need to specify two parameters):

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
rnbinom(n = 10, size = 5)
```

-   In the case above, we need the argument `prob` (i.e., parameter $p$ in the Negative Binomial distribution). `R` will indicate that `prob` is missing.

#### Another way to use `rnbinom()` in `R`!

<br>

-   Recall the expected value of a Negative Binomial random variable is

$$\mu = \mathbb{E}(X) = \frac{k(1 - p)}{p} = \frac{5(1 - 0.6)}{0.6} = 3.33.$$

. . .

-   From `lecture2`, we know that a distribution [can also be parameterized]{style="color: purple;"} with its corresponding mean.

</br>

#### Therefore...

-   We can use the the argument `mu` in the random number generator `rnbinom()`. Note `mu` refers to $\mu = \mathbb{E}(X)$:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
rnbinom(n = 10, size = 5, mu = 3.33)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
rnbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.6)
```

. . .

-   We get the same random numbers via the same seed!

### iClicker Question

Suppose you want to simulate hourly bank branch queues of customers. **Historically**, hourly queues show an average of 10 people. 

What distribution (including parametrization) and `R` random number generator will you use to simulate 20 random numbers?

#### Select the correct option:

<br>

**A.** $\text{Poisson}(\lambda = 1/10)$ with 

`rpois(n = 20, lambda = 1 / 10)`

**B.** $\text{Binomial}(n = 10, p = 1/10)$ with 

`rbinom(n = 20, size = 10, prob = 1 / 10)`

**C.** $\text{Poisson}(\lambda = 10)$ with 

`rpois(n = 20, lambda = 10)`

**D.** $\text{Geometric}(p = 1/10)$ with 

`rgeom(n = 20, prob = 1 / 10)`

### iClicker Question

During a random foodie tour, suppose you want to simulate the number of non-authentic Mexican restaurants you will try before encountering your very first authentic one in Vancouver. Overall, **it is known that 70% of Mexican restaurants in Vancouver are considered non-authentic** (but you do not have access to this list!).

What distribution (including parametrization) and `R` random number generator will you use to simulate 15 random numbers?

#### Select the correct option:

<br>

**A.** $\text{Binomial}(n = 15, p = 0.7)$ with 

`rbinom(n = 15, size = 15, prob = 0.7)`

**B.** $\text{Geometric}(p = 0.3)$ with 

`rgeom(n = 15, prob = 0.3)`

**C.** $\text{Binomial}(n = 15, p = 0.3)$ with 

`rbinom(n = 15, size = 15, prob = 0.3)`

**D.** $\text{Geometric}(p = 0.7)$ with 

`rgeom(n = 15, prob = 0.7)`

## 4. Running Simulations

![](images/crab.png){.absolute top="-80" right="-80" width="20%"}

. . .

-   So far, we have discussed two ways to calculate quantities that help us communicate uncertainty (like means and probabilities):

. . .

1.  The [distribution-based approach]{style="color: purple;"} (using the distribution), resulting in [true values]{style="color: purple;"}.
2.  The [empirical approach]{style="color: purple;"} (using data), resulting in [approximate values]{style="color: purple;"} that improve as the sample size increases ([i.e., the frequentist paradigm!]{style="color: purple;"}).

### The Mean

-   The [true]{style="color: purple;"} mean of a discrete random variable $X$ can be calculated as $$\mathbb{E}(X) = \sum_x x \cdot P(X = x).$$

-   Or can be approximated using the [empirical]{style="color: purple;"} approach from a random sample $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ by $$\mathbb{E}(X) \approx \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i.$$

### 4.1. Code for Empirical Quantities

-   Here are some `R` functions to calculate empirical quantities:
    -   `mean()` calculates the [sample average]{style="color: purple;"} $$\bar{X} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n X_i.$$
    -   `var()` calculates the [sample variance]{style="color: purple;"} $$S^2 = \frac{1}{n-1} \sum_{i=1}^n (X_i - \bar{X})^2.$$

#### Furthermore...

-   `quantile()` calculates the [empirical $p$-quantile]{style="color: purple;"}: the $np$'th largest (rounded up) observation in a sample of size $n$.
-   For a single probability, calculate the mean of a condition.

. . .

-   For an [entire PMF]{style="color: purple;"}, use the `table()` function, or more conveniently, the `janitor::tabyl()` function.
-   For the mode, either get it manually using the `table()` or `janitor::tabyl()` function, or you can use `DescTools::Mode()`.

### 4.2. Basic Simulation

-   In Mexico City, consider a [random person]{style="color: purple;"} dating via [some given app]{style="color: purple;"} with a probability of having a successful date of $0.7$.

![[The Angel of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angel_of_Independence), one of the most famous landmarks in Mexico City with a [Jacaranda tree](https://mexiconewsdaily.com/news/purple-spring-5-fun-facts-about-jacarandas/) closeup (photo by <a href="https://unsplash.com/@axelgarcia?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText">Axel García</a> on <a href="https://unsplash.com/photos/yWgIfYgwVfA?utm_source=unsplash&utm_medium=referral&utm_content=creditCopyText">Unsplash</a>).](images/angel.jpg){height="310"}

#### Also...

-   Suppose we want to evaluate the success of this given app via the [number of failed dates]{style="color: purple;"} before they experience $5$ [successful dates]{style="color: purple;"}.

. . .

-   We can translate the above inquiry as a random variable denoting failed dates has a Negative Binomial distribution: \begin{align*}
    X &= \text{Number of failed dates before experiencing} \\
    & \qquad \text{5 successful ones} \\
    \end{align*} $$X \sim \text{Negative Binomial} (k = 5, p = 0.7) \quad \text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, ...$$

#### Obtaining our random sample...

-   Let us demonstrate both a distribution-based and empirical approach to compute the variance and PMF.
-   First, let us obtain our random sample (of, say, $n = 10000$ observations).

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551)
k <- 5
p <- 0.7
n <- 10000
random_sample <- rnbinom(n, size = k, prob = p)
head(random_sample, 30) # Showing the first 30 random numbers in vector random_sample
```

#### 4.2.1. Mean

-   [Theoretically]{style="color: purple;"}, the mean of $X$ is $\mathbb{E}(X) = \frac{k(1 - p)}{p}$.
-   We compute it as follows:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
(k * (1 - p)) / p
```

. . .

-   [Empirically]{style="color: purple;"}, we can approximate $\mathbb{E}(X)$ with the mean of the values in `random_sample`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
mean(random_sample)
```

#### 4.2.2. Variance

-   [Theoretically]{style="color: purple;"}, the variance of $X$ is $\text{Var}(X) = \frac{k(1 - p)}{p^2}$.
-   We compute it as follows:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
(k * (1 - p)) / p^2
```

. . .

-   [Empirically]{style="color: purple;"}, we can approximate $\text{Var}(X)$ with the sample variance of the values in `random_sample`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
var(random_sample)
```

#### 4.2.3. Standard deviation

-   [Theoretically]{style="color: purple;"}, the standard deviation of $X$ is $\text{sd}(X) = \sqrt{\frac{k(1 - p)}{p^2}}$.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
sqrt((1 - p) * k / p^2)
```

. . .

-   [Empirically]{style="color: purple;"}, we can approximate $\text{sd}(X)$ with the sample standard deviation of the values in `random_sample`:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
sd(random_sample)
```

#### 4.2.4. Probability of Seeing $0$ Failures (i.e., $0$ failed dates!)

-   [Theoretically]{style="color: purple;"}, this probability can be computed as

$$
P(X = 0 \mid k, p) = {k - 1 \choose 0} p^k (1 - p)^x.
$$

. . .

-   We can automatically compute this probability via the density function `dnbinom()` as follows:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
dnbinom(x = 0, size = k, prob = p)
```

#### [Empirically]{style="color: purple;"}...

-   We can approximate $P(X = 0 \mid k = 5, p = 0.7)$ by [counting the number of random numbers equal to $0$ in `random_sample`]{style="color: purple;"} and dividing this count over the sample size $n = 10000$.

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
head(random_sample) # First 6 random numbers out of 10000
head(random_sample == 0) # First 6 logical values out of 10000
mean(random_sample == 0) # Using function mean()
```

#### 4.2.5. Probability Mass Function

-   Just as we did it with $P(X = 0 \mid k = 5, p = 0.7)$, we can also do it for $P(X = i \mid k = 5, p = 0.7)$ with $i = 1, 2, \dots$ (i.e., [the whole PMF!]{style="color: purple;"}).

. . .

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)

PMF <- tabyl(random_sample) |>
  select(x = random_sample, Empirical = percent) |>
  mutate(Theoretical = dnbinom(x, size = k, prob = p))
PMF <- PMF |>
  mutate(
    Theoretical = round(Theoretical, 4),
    Empirical = round(Empirical, 4)
  )
```

#### Showing the output `PMF`

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
PMF
```

-   Note that both probability columns are similar!

#### Plotting both PMFs

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

library(janitor)

set.seed(551)
k <- 5
p <- 0.7
n <- 10000
random_sample <- rnbinom(n, size = k, prob = p)

PMF <- tabyl(random_sample) |>
  select(x = random_sample, Empirical = percent) |>
  mutate(Theoretical = dnbinom(x, size = k, prob = p))
PMF <- PMF |>
  mutate(
    Theoretical = round(Theoretical, 4),
    Empirical = round(Empirical, 4)
  )

PMF |>
  gather(key = "method", value = "Probability", Empirical, Theoretical) |>
  ggplot(aes(x, Probability)) +
  facet_wrap(~method) +
  geom_col(fill = "maroon") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold")) +
  ggtitle("Comparison of Empirical and Theoretical PMFs") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:12) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25))
```

#### 4.2.6. Mode

-   Recall the mode is the outcome of the random variable with the [largest probability]{style="color: purple;"}.
-   From our previous plots, we can see that it is $X = 1.$

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
## Theoretical
PMF |> filter(Theoretical == max(Theoretical)) |>
  pull(x)
```

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
## Empirical
PMF |> filter(Empirical == max(Empirical)) |>
  pull(x)
```

#### 4.2.6. The Law of Large Numbers

-   The Law of Large of Numbers states that, as we increase our sample size $n$, our empirical mean converges to the [true mean]{style="color: purple;"} we want to estimate.
-   That is, as we increase our $n$, our [sample average]{style="color: purple;"} $\bar{X}$ converges to the true mean $\mu$.

. . .

-   Let us exemplify this: \begin{gather*}
    X \sim \text{Negative Binomial} (k = 5, p = 0.7) \quad \text{with} \\
    \mathbb{E}(X) = \frac{k(1 - p)}{p} = 2.14.
    \end{gather*}

#### Increasing the sample size $n$

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

tibble(
  i = 1:n,
  mean = cumsum(random_sample) / i
) |>
  ggplot(aes(i, mean)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = (1 - p) * k / p,
    colour = "maroon", linetype = "dashed", size = 0.75
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Sample Size",
    y = "Empirical Mean"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold")) +
  ggtitle("Evolution of Empirical Mean as Sample Size is Increased") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 3, 0.25)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 10000, 1000))
```

## 5. Multi-Step Simulations

-   The previous univariate simulation might seem [trivial]{style="color: purple;"}, since we could calculate basically anything (theoretically speaking!).
-   Where it gets more interesting is [when we want to calculate things for a random variable that transforms and/or combines multiple random variables]{style="color: purple;"}.

![](images/panda.png){fig-align="center" width="20%"}

### For example...

-   Consider a random variable $T$ that we can obtain as follows: \begin{gather*}
    X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda = 5) \\
    T = \sum_{i = 1}^{X} D_i.
    \end{gather*}

-   Where each $D_i$ are *iid* with [some specified distribution]{style="color: purple;"}.

-   In this case, you would first need to generate $X$, then generate $X$ values of $D_i$, then sum those up to get $T$.

### The Port of Vancouver

-   Consider an example that a Vancouver port faces with [gang demand]{style="color: purple;"}.
-   Whenever a ship arrives to the port of Vancouver, they request a certain number of [gangs]{style="color: purple;"} (groups of people) to help unload the ship.

![](images/ship.png){fig-align="center" width="30%"}

#### Looking at the PMF!

![](images/sea-condition.png){.absolute top="-80" right="0" width="30%"}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 7

gang <- 1:4
p <- c(0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1)

tibble(
  gangs = gang,
  p     = p
) |>
  ggplot(aes(gangs, p)) +
  geom_col(fill = "palegreen3") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Gangs",
    y = "Probability"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold")) +
  ggtitle("PMF of Number of Gangs")
```

#### Coding up a simulation function!

<br>

-   The following function sums up simulated gangs requested by a certain number of ships with the above probability distribution as a default.

</br>

#### `R` Function

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
#' Generate gang demand
#'
#' Simulates the GRAND TOTAL number of gangs requested, if each ship
#' requests a random number of gangs.
#' 
#' @param n_ships Number of ships that are making demands.
#' @param gangs Possible gang demands made by a ship.
#' @param prob Probabilities of gang demand corresponding to "gangs."
#' 
#' @return Number representing the total gang demand 
demand_gangs <- function(n_ships, gangs = 1:4, prob = c(0.2, 0.4, 0.3, 0.1)) {
  if (length(gangs) == 1) {
    gangs <- c(gangs)
    prob <- c(1)
  }
  requests <- sample(
    gangs,
    size = n_ships,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = prob
  )
  sum(requests)
}
```

#### Using `demand_gangs()`

<br>

-   As an example, let us check out the simulated [grand total gang request]{style="color: purple;"} from 10 ships:

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
set.seed(551) # Reproducibility
demand_gangs(n_ships = 10)
```

. . .

-   Now, suppose that the number of ships arriving on a given day follows a [Poisson distribution with a mean of $\lambda = 5 \text{ ships}$]{style="color: purple;"}.

</br>

# What is the distribution of total gang requests on a given day?

#### Let us simulate the process to find out!

![](images/sea-condition.png){.absolute top="-60" right="0" width="25%"}

<br>

::: incremental
1.  Generate arrival quantities for $n$ days from the $\text{Poisson}(\lambda = 5 \text{ ships})$ distribution.
2.  For each day, simulate [the grand total gang request]{style="color: purple;"} for the simulated number of ships.
3.  You now have your random sample of size $n$; compute things as you normally would.
:::

. . .

-   Let us try this, obtaining [a sample of $n = 10000$ days]{style="color: purple;"}.

</br>

#### The Code

![](images/code.png){.absolute top="-30" right="0" width="5%"}

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
n_days <- 10000

# Setting global seed!
set.seed(551)

## Step 1: generate a bunch of ships arriving each day.
arrivals <- rpois(n_days, lambda = 5)
head(arrivals)
```

#### Then...

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
## Step 2: Simulate the grand total gang request on each day.
total_requests <- purrr::map_int(arrivals, demand_gangs)
head(total_requests)
```

#### Finally

```{webr}
#| autorun: true
## Step 3: Compute mean and variance.
simulation_outputs <- tibble(
  mean = mean(total_requests),
  variance = var(total_requests)
)
simulation_outputs
```

. . .

-   From our $n = 10000$ replicates, the summary statistics above indicate that [we typically expect a demand of 11.5 gangs on a given day in the whole port]{style="color: purple;"}.

### Checking the empirical distribution of total gang requests!

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11.5
#| fig-height: 6

#' Generate gang demand
#'
#' Simulates the GRAND TOTAL number of gangs requested, if each ship
#' requests a random number of gangs.
#' 
#' @param n_ships Number of ships that are making demands.
#' @param gangs Possible gang demands made by a ship.
#' @param prob Probabilities of gang demand corresponding to "gangs."
#' 
#' @return Number representing the total gang demand 
demand_gangs <- function(n_ships, gangs = gang, prob = p) {
  if (length(gangs) == 1) {
    gangs <- c(gangs, gangs)
    prob <- c(1, 1)
  }
  requests <- sample(
    gangs,
    size = n_ships,
    replace = TRUE,
    prob = prob
  )
  sum(requests)
}

# Simualtion
n_days <- 10000
set.seed(551)
arrivals <- rpois(n_days, lambda = 5)
total_requests <- purrr::map_int(arrivals, demand_gangs)
total_requests <- data.frame(sim = total_requests)

# Plotting
ggplot(total_requests, aes(sim)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "orange") +
  labs(
    x = "Number of Gangs",
    y = "Counts"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold"),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 16, face = "bold"),
    strip.text.x = element_text(size = 17, face = "bold")) +
  ggtitle("Simulation Results") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 40, 5)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 11.5393, color = "blue", size = 1.5)
```

## Final Block Wrap Up

-   Even though probability is an abstract field, we will often use these tools throughout the program.
-   Having a good knowledge of random variable distributions is an expected asset in data modelling.
-   As Data Scientists, you need to be able to communicate your findings via adequate summaries.
